conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers to be sure they’re getting the emotional support they need after delivery.

Over the next few minutes I’m going to walk you through a short questionnaire called the EPDS—that stands for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a simple, 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past week. These questions don’t replace a full clinical interview, but they give us a quick snapshot of how you’re coping in this early postpartum period.

Everything you share with me today is confidential, and your answers stay between you and your care team. There are no right or wrong responses—just whatever feels true for you right now. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause or take a break. When we finish, we’ll look at the results together and talk about next steps, resources, or anything else that might be helpful.

We’ll keep it conversational: I’ll ask each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels easiest. Ready to start?

Here’s the first question:

In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult for you?

I guess I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband does something silly with the baby—but it doesn’t feel as easy as it used to. Mostly I’m just tired, so even things that should be funny feel like they take extra effort.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, just not as often or as freely as before. It’s like I have to remind myself, “This is funny—laugh,” instead of it just happening naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can take a shower without rushing—but it’s more because I know I’ll feel relief, not real excitement. The only thing I actually anticipate with any joy is maybe a quiet cup of coffee, and even that feels small.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like last night the baby wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept thinking maybe I’d eaten something wrong or wasn’t holding him right. Rationally I know babies just cry, but the little voice in my head still whispers that I should have figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not gaining enough weight, or I’ll lie down and picture her stopping breathing in the bassinet. Nothing sets it off—just this constant low-level fear something will go wrong and I won’t catch it in time.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… it’s like a sudden wave of “something bad is about to happen.” Last night I was walking to the kitchen for a glass of water and my chest got tight, heart pounding, for no reason at all. It passes after a minute, but it leaves me shaky and watching the baby monitor like crazy.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. Between feedings, diapers, and trying to grab a shower, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I keep lists, but the second I cross something off, two more things pile on. I’m not falling apart, but I end the day exhausted and already dreading tomorrow.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy,” just kind of flat and wound up at the same time. When I finally lie down, my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles, is she breathing, why hasn’t she pooped today—so it takes forever to drift off. I probably manage only three or four solid hours a night, then I’m up every hour after that.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like this heavy, achy feeling that shows up out of nowhere. It’s not constant, but it hits especially in the evenings when the house gets quiet and I’m finally sitting down. I end up tearing up for a minute, then I push it aside because I know I have to stay functional for the baby.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I get teary maybe once or twice a week, but the tears don’t actually fall most of the time. It’s more this pressure behind my eyes that never turns into full crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My mind is too focused on keeping my baby safe to even go there.

I hear how hard you're working to stay afloat, juggling constant feedings, nappies, and the endless mental checklist that keeps you awake at night. You shared that laughter now feels forced, tiny reliefs like a quiet cup of coffee bring only fleeting comfort, and waves of fear or panic catch you off-guard. Yet through it all your protective love for your baby shines, and you still find ways to push through each day.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh spontaneously, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>She can still anticipate tiny reliefs but explicitly denies "real excitement" and describes only minimal joy, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame 'sometimes' and gives a specific example, aligning with 'Yes, some of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, catastrophic worries without triggers, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic attack symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, sudden fear) occurring frequently, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and exhaustion, indicating difficulty coping "most days" but not complete inability to function, aligning with "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient denies being "so unhappy" but describes persistent nighttime rumination and fragmented sleep, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 18 places you well above the 14-point cut-off indicating probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset. Your answers map to five key areas: diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), excessive self-blame (<sym>guilt</sym>), daily anxiety and repeated panic symptoms, sleep disruption not solely due to infant care, and feeling overwhelmed most days. Together these meet core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, though a full clinical interview is required to confirm. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent follow-up with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist for full evaluation
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments for postpartum depression such as <med>CBT</med>, peer-support groups, or medication options compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share today's score with your <med>OB-GYN</med> at your next visit so it can be tracked
4. Practise brief breathing techniques when panic sensations start; pair with grounding exercises to calm racing thoughts
5. Accept practical help overnight if available so you can obtain four-hour stretches of sleep-improving rest can boost mood and reduce anxiety
6. Keep a simple daily log of mood, sleep, and anxiety spikes to review with your clinician at follow-up
7. Involve your partner or trusted support person in baby-care shifts to lower the constant sense of being "on alert"
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  
Source: Patient self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire (10 items)

Symptoms / Concerns  
- Anhedonia: reduced spontaneous laughter; anticipates only minor relief (quiet coffee) rather than pleasure  
- Excessive guilt: self-blame when infant fusses  
- Persistent anxiety: daily “low-level fear,” spontaneous panic episodes (tight chest, racing heart)  
- Overwhelm: feels perpetually behind, dreads next day  
- Mood-congruent insomnia: 3–4 h initial sleep, then hourly wakings ruminating about infant safety  
- Intermittent sad / “flat” mood, evening tearfulness  
- No anhedonia-independent sleep issues, appetite, or concentration data reported  
- Denies self-harm ideation (endorsed Q10 “No—never”)

Pattern  
Moderate but persistent distress beginning post-delivery; symptoms present most days; functional impact on sleep, mood regulation, and sense of mastery; no psychotic or suicidal features.

Screening Significance  
EPDS responses consistent with probable minor–moderate postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; meets threshold items for further evaluation (anhedonia, guilt, anxiety, sleep, overwhelm).

Risk Factors  
- Sleep deprivation linked to mood disturbance  
- High self-expectations / guilt  
- Spontaneous panic symptoms

Safety  
No expressed suicidal or infanticidal ideation; no self-harm intent or plan.

Next Steps  
Recommend formal clinical interview (EPDS follow-up or PHQ-9/GAD-7) and consideration of referral to perinatal mental-health specialty services for assessment and possible evidence-based intervention.
